title: Holding Costs and Rehab Timelines for Investors
metaDescription: What makes up holding costs on a rehab, what causes schedule slip, how to sequence trades, and practical ways investors protect the timeline to exit.
h1: Holding Costs and Rehab Timelines: What Drives the Clock and How to Protect It
dek: Holding costs are everything you pay to own a property while it is not producing income: interest, taxes, insurance, utilities, maintenance and the cost of your own capital. Every day of schedule slip adds to them, so protecting a rehab timeline is as much about planning, sequencing and fast decisions as about the work itself.
keyTakeaways: Holding costs run every day from closing to sale or stabilized rent, whether or not anyone is working on site.
Schedule slip usually comes from a small set of causes: incomplete scope, late permits, material lead times, trade gaps, slow decisions and failed inspections.
Sequencing trades correctly, especially around rough-in inspections, prevents idle days and rework.
The pre-construction period, between offer and demolition, is where much of the timeline is won or lost.
Draw schedules, change-order approvals and selections are owner-side tasks that can delay a job as much as anything on site.

sections.h2: What counts as a holding cost?
sections.body:
Holding costs are the expenses of owning a property during the period it is not earning, which on a flip runs from purchase to sale and on a BRRRR or rental runs from purchase to stabilized occupancy or refinance. They accrue every day regardless of how much work happens.

The main components:
- Financing costs: interest on acquisition and rehab loans, plus any extension fees if the loan term runs past its original maturity
- Opportunity cost of your own capital: cash in the deal that could be working elsewhere
- Property taxes, prorated for the holding period, and in some jurisdictions reassessed after purchase or renovation
- Insurance: a builder's risk or vacant dwelling policy during the rehab, which can be priced differently from a standard homeowner or landlord policy
- Utilities: electric, gas, water and sewer, trash, and sometimes temporary service needed during construction
- HOA or condo fees where applicable
- Maintenance and security: lawn care, snow removal, winterization, security measures and periodic inspections while the house is vacant
- Vacant property registration fees in jurisdictions that require them

Some investors also count marketing and staging during the listing period, since the house is still being held while it is on the market.

Holding costs are easy to underestimate because each one looks small and they arrive as separate bills. Added together over the full hold, they are a meaningful part of the deal's cost. That is why the timeline belongs in the offer analysis, not just in the construction plan.

sections.h2: How should you estimate holding costs in your offer?
sections.body:
Estimate holding costs from the start, using a realistic timeline that covers the whole hold, not just construction.

Break the hold into phases:
- Closing to start of work: permitting, final scope, contractor mobilization and any utility setup
- Construction: demolition through final inspections and punch list
- Exit: for a flip, listing preparation, time on market and closing; for a rental, leasing and move-in; for a BRRRR, leasing, seasoning periods if your lender requires them, appraisal and refinance closing

For each phase, list the costs that apply and estimate a daily or monthly carrying figure. Interest, taxes, insurance and utilities usually apply throughout. Some costs change by phase, such as switching from builder's risk to a landlord policy when tenants move in.

Then stress-test it. What happens to the deal if construction runs longer than planned, or the house sits on the market longer? If the deal only works on the most optimistic timeline, it is fragile. Build in a timeline contingency the same way you build in a budget contingency.

Use local information. Permit review times, inspector availability, seasonal construction conditions and typical marketing times vary by city and by season. A contractor and agent who work the market can tell you what is typical there.

Genstone's free Pre-Offer Rehab Review looks at repair costs and ARV before you commit; folding a realistic schedule into that review gives you the full carrying picture before you make the offer.

sections.h2: What causes rehab schedules to slip?
sections.body:
Most slipped schedules can be traced to a short list of causes. Knowing them is the first step to preventing them.

Incomplete or vague scope. If the scope does not define what is being done in each room, decisions get made on site, materials get ordered late and change orders pile up.

Hidden conditions. Rot, failed drains, outdated wiring, foundation issues and a damaged sewer lateral add work and sometimes require new permits or engineering.

Permits and plan review. Work that needs drawings or review can take time to approve, and late-discovered permit requirements stop work that was already underway.

Material lead times. Special-order cabinets, windows, doors, appliances and some tile or flooring can take longer than expected to arrive, and a single late item can hold up several trades.

Trade availability and gaps. When one trade finishes and the next is not ready, the house sits. Busy seasons make this worse.

Failed inspections. A failed rough inspection delays drywall and everything after it until corrections are made and re-inspected.

Owner decisions. Late selections, slow change-order approvals and changes of mind on finishes or layout are among the most common causes of delay that investors do not count.

Draw and payment delays. If draws are slow to be inspected and released, contractors may slow down or move crews to other jobs.

Weather and season. Exterior work, roofing, concrete and excavation are weather-dependent, and frozen ground, heavy rain and extreme heat affect what can be done.

Utilities. Getting service turned on, upgraded or separated can depend on the utility's schedule rather than yours.

Few of these are entirely outside your control. Most can be reduced with planning done before work begins.

sections.h2: How should trades be sequenced on a rehab?
sections.body:
Trade sequencing is the order in which work happens. The goal is to keep each trade working continuously and to avoid any trade damaging or undoing another's work.

A typical sequence for a substantial interior rehab:
- Cleanout and demolition, including any hazardous material abatement and lead-safe containment
- Structural repairs and framing changes
- Rough plumbing, rough electrical and rough HVAC, with exterior penetrations for vents and lines
- Windows and exterior doors, which can often be done in parallel with rough-ins
- Rough inspections
- Insulation and any insulation inspection
- Drywall hanging, taping and finishing
- Prime and first coat of paint
- Cabinets, then countertop templating and installation
- Tile and flooring, often with tile before cabinets in some layouts and hard flooring after paint
- Trim and doors
- Finish plumbing, finish electrical and HVAC trim-out
- Appliances
- Final paint and touch-up
- Final inspections, punch list and final clean

Exterior work such as roofing, siding, gutters, concrete and landscaping usually runs in parallel, weather permitting. Roofing early protects the interior; landscaping late avoids damage from construction traffic.

Key dependencies to respect: drywall cannot start until rough inspections pass; countertops cannot be templated until cabinets are installed; finish plumbing and electrical cannot be done until surfaces are finished. These are where idle days happen if the next trade is not ready.

On bigger jobs, overlap trades across areas. A drywall crew can finish one floor while electricians rough in another. A manager tracking the whole job should be looking a few steps ahead at all times.

sections.h2: Why is the pre-construction period so important?
sections.body:
Many investors think of the timeline as starting when demolition starts. In practice, much of the schedule is won or lost before anyone swings a hammer.

Use the period between accepted offer and closing, and between closing and mobilization, to do the following:
- Finalize scope in detail, room by room, with finish selections, quantities and exclusions
- Identify permit-required work and submit applications as early as the jurisdiction allows
- Order long-lead materials, such as windows, cabinets, specialty doors, appliances and any special-order finishes
- Book trades with tentative dates based on the sequence
- Arrange utilities so power and water are on for construction
- Set up the draw schedule with your lender and understand their inspection process
- Plan dumpster placement, site access and any neighbor or HOA notification
- Confirm insurance coverage for the construction period

Scope completeness is the single biggest factor. A detailed scope reduces mid-project decisions, makes ordering possible before demolition and gives every trade a clear picture of their work. It also makes change orders easier to identify and price.

Selections are the second biggest. If you have not chosen cabinets, counters, tile, flooring, fixtures and paint before work starts, someone will be waiting on you at some point. Finish selections, or at least a firm specification and allowances, should be done before mobilization.

The less that has to be figured out once the house is open, the faster it moves.

sections.h2: How do draws and decisions affect the timeline?
sections.body:
The owner is part of the schedule. Some of the most common delays happen on the owner's side, not in the field.

Draws. If your rehab is financed with a loan that holds back construction funds, the lender typically releases money in draws after an inspection confirms work is complete. The process can involve submitting a draw request, scheduling the lender's inspector, reviewing photos and releasing funds. If any step is slow, contractors may wait for payment before ordering materials or continuing work. Understand your lender's draw process before work starts, align the contractor's draw schedule to the lender's milestones, and submit requests promptly with good documentation.

Change orders. When a hidden condition appears, a fast, documented change-order decision keeps crews working. A decision that sits unanswered for days stops the affected trade and sometimes the trades behind it. Agree in advance who approves changes, what documentation you need, and how quickly you will respond.

Selections. Late or changed selections cause reorders, returns and rework. Make decisions once and stick to them.

Access and communication. Make sure the contractor has keys, codes and any HOA approvals. Respond to questions quickly. If you cannot be on site, rely on photo and video updates and set a regular reporting cadence.

Genstone ties construction draws to completed work and keeps progress and documentation visible without the client being on site. Arrangements like that work best when owner-side decisions keep pace with the field.

sections.h2: How do season and weather affect rehab timing?
sections.body:
Seasons affect both construction and the exit, and the effect differs by region.

Construction. In cold climates, winter limits exterior work: roofing, siding, concrete, excavation, sewer lateral replacement and exterior paint can be difficult or impossible during deep cold or when the ground is frozen. Interior work continues, but vacant houses need heat to protect pipes and allow paint, drywall compound and flooring adhesives to cure properly. In hot climates, summer heat affects crew productivity and some materials, and storm seasons interrupt exterior work. Wet seasons anywhere slow excavation, foundation work and drying.

Plan exterior scope for favorable weather. If you close in late fall in a northern market, prioritize roof and exterior envelope work immediately and leave interior finishes for winter. In a hurricane-prone market, get the envelope closed before the peak of storm season.

Trade availability also follows the seasons. Busy building seasons mean trades are booked further out and lead times stretch.

Exit. Buyer demand varies through the year in many markets, often with more activity in spring and early summer and less around the winter holidays, though patterns differ by region and price range. A flip that slips past its intended listing window may face a slower market. For rentals, leasing demand also follows seasonal patterns, particularly in markets with school-year or university-driven moves.

When you plan your timeline, map it to the calendar. Knowing when the house is likely to list or lease tells you how much schedule risk you can afford.

sections.h2: What are the most effective ways to protect the timeline?
sections.body:
A short list of habits prevents most schedule slip.

Before purchase:
- Investigate what you can, including permit history, a sewer scope, and a close look at systems and structure
- Build a realistic timeline into the offer, including a timeline contingency

Before construction:
- Write a complete, room-by-room scope with selections and exclusions
- Submit permits early and order long-lead materials
- Book trades in sequence with a manager who owns the schedule
- Set up the draw process and the change-order process in writing

During construction:
- Hold a regular check-in on progress, the next steps, upcoming inspections and any open decisions
- Approve change orders quickly on documented evidence
- Pre-walk work before inspections to avoid failures
- Keep the next trade ready before the current one finishes
- Track materials still to arrive and their expected dates

At exit:
- Prepare listing or leasing materials while finishes are being completed
- Schedule photography as soon as the house is clean and staged
- Have documentation ready, including permits finaled, warranties and receipts, for buyers, appraisers and lenders

The pattern is that the timeline is protected by preparation and decisions more than by working faster on site. A crew can only work as quickly as the scope, materials, permits, inspections and approvals allow. When those are lined up ahead of time, the work itself tends to move at a steady pace, and steady is what keeps holding costs predictable.

faqs.q: What are typical holding costs on a fix and flip?
faqs.a: The categories are consistent even though amounts vary widely by market, loan and property: loan interest and fees, property taxes, insurance during construction and listing, utilities, HOA dues where applicable, maintenance and security while vacant, vacant property registration where required, and the opportunity cost of your own cash. Estimate each on a daily or monthly basis for your specific deal and multiply by a realistic timeline that includes marketing and closing, not just construction.

faqs.q: What is the most common reason rehabs run late?
faqs.a: Incomplete scope is the root cause behind many delays. When rooms, finishes, quantities and exclusions are not defined before work starts, decisions are made on site, materials are ordered late, and change orders multiply. Hidden conditions, permit delays, material lead times and slow owner decisions are also common. Most of these can be reduced by investing time in scope, selections, permits and ordering before demolition begins.

faqs.q: Can I speed up a rehab by running trades at the same time?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Trades working in different areas or on independent tasks, such as exterior work alongside interior rough-ins, or drywall on one floor while another floor is roughed in, can overlap well. Trades that depend on each other cannot, such as drywall before rough inspections pass or countertops before cabinets are set. Forcing overlaps creates damage and rework. A manager who understands the dependencies can find the safe overlaps.

faqs.q: How do loan draws affect a rehab timeline?
faqs.a: Draws release rehab funds after work is verified complete. If the lender's inspection and payment process is slow, contractors may wait to order materials or proceed, which slows the job. Align the contractor's draw schedule with your lender's milestones, understand the inspection process before work starts, and submit draw requests promptly with photos and documentation so funds release on time.

faqs.q: Should I avoid starting a rehab in winter?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. In cold climates, winter limits exterior work like roofing, concrete and excavation, and vacant houses need heat to protect pipes and allow finishes to cure. Interior work can proceed normally with heat on, and trades may be more available. Plan the sequence around the season: close the exterior envelope before deep cold if possible, and time the finish so the listing or leasing lands in a stronger season.
